paragraphs: Should we teach people to fall on their knees and call themselves miserable sinners? Swamiji's answer was no. Far better, he said, to remind them of the divinity within, and he told a story to make the point.

A lioness, hunting for food, came upon a flock of sheep. As she sprang at one of them, she gave birth to a cub and died right there. The little lion grew up among the sheep. He nibbled grass, bleated like they did, and had no idea what he really was.

Years later, another lion passed by and could hardly believe his eyes: a huge lion grazing and bleating in the middle of the flock! When the sheep saw the newcomer, they all ran, and the lion-sheep ran with them. But the stranger waited patiently, and one day found the lion-sheep asleep.

He woke him and told him he was a lion. The lion-sheep refused to believe it and simply bleated back. So the stranger led him to a lake and asked him to look at his reflection in the water. Did he not look just like the stranger? The lion-sheep had to admit he did. Then the stranger roared and asked him to try. The young lion tested his voice, and soon he was roaring every bit as mightily. He was never a sheep again.

Swamiji told his listeners that they too were mighty as lions. When a room is dark, he said, there is no use crying about the darkness; you strike a light and it disappears. In the same way, kindle the spiritual light within, and weakness and impurity will vanish.
learn: Many of us carry labels we picked up from others: average, weak, not good enough. Spend less energy mourning your faults and more energy discovering your real strength; the darkness goes the moment you light the lamp.
